newsitem.title: CHINA: China seen buying soybeans, meal on price dips.
newsitem.headline: China seen buying soybeans, meal on price dips.

text.p: China has been buying soybeans and soybean meal on recent price dips, picking up about half a million tonnes of beans and up to 350,000 tonnes of soybean meal in the past month, Far East traders said on Wednesday.
China had become a consistent, smart and predictable buyer of soy complex products and the buys came as no surprise, they said.
Sales early this week totalled at least 50,000 tonnes of soybean meal as Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) prices tumbled below $300 a tonne, a trader in Singapore said.
The old crop, optional Brazil/Argentina cargoes sold at around $297 a tonne for nearby delivery, he said, adding that some of his customers had already opened letters of credit.
With domestic Chinese soybean meal prices yet to move below 2,800 yuan ($337) a tonne, the imported product would arrive at 2,700 yuan ($325), giving sellers a healthy margin, he said.
"As long as there is a margin, the Chinese will buy," he said.
Credit was being furiously organised as genuine buyers, and some speculators, scurried for money to take advantage of the market opportunities, the traders said.
Another trading source said last week's total soybean meal purchases were between 200,000 and 300,000 tonnes. Monday's 50,000 tonnes brought the total to 350,000 tonnes on the upside, he said.
Bean purchases of both old and new crop were around 500,000 tonnes on the upside, he said. No other details were available.
"As long as the domestic price maintains this level, why not buy?" another trading source said.
"Until there is physical delivery you will not see the domestic price pushed down, and unless you see physical pressure there is no reason for domestic prices to fall," he said.
Arrivals due to begin in 50 days would coincide with China's peak feed consumption period -- a coincidence likely to keep prices bouyant, traders said.
"So the question is which will be heavier -- demand or deliveries," he said.

China bought at least 200,000 tonnes each of soybeans and soybean meal early last week when CBOT prices dipped on good weather news. At that time, some trading sources put possible meal purchases at 500,000 to 800,000 tonnes, but these quantities could not be confirmed.
Buying interest waned after those purchases sent prices back up -- although another 58,000 tonnes of soybean meal was reported sold last Wednesday in three lots.
Price dips on Monday brought Chinese buyers back to the market, the traders said.
Traders said the waves of bean buying, which began with joint venture mills, and was followed up on the second price dip by state-run companies, could be expected to continue.
One of the Singapore traders said bean buying totalled 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, but this was considered an exaggeration by some other trading sources.
A supply-related rally in CBOT soybeans pushed soymeal and soyoil futures to end with moderate gains on Tuesday, floor traders said.
CBOT July soybeans settled 14-1/2 cents per bushel higher on concerns over scant U.S. supplies and fears that the El Nino effect will produce drought in some countries this year, they said.
-- Shanghai Newsroom (8621) 6279-8544
